summary:
Workplace Insight reports on economic modelling from International Workplace Group (IWG) and Arup arguing that hybrid working could generate substantial productivity gains, primarily through improved staff retention. The modelling estimates retention-linked gains worth $204.7 billion to the US economy and £10.8 billion to the UK over five years, making retention the largest single source of projected benefit. The argument is that lower turnover preserves experience, institutional knowledge and productive capacity, not just recruitment cost savings. Reduced disruption from lost organisational knowledge is valued at $65.5 billion (US) and £5.7 billion (UK) over five years, improved talent attraction at $98.3 billion and £6.5 billion, and recruitment and onboarding efficiencies at $9.4 billion and £600 million.

IWG also cites survey research on flexibility as a recruitment lever: 81 percent of chief human resources officers said hybrid working was important for retaining top talent, and 86 percent identified flexible working as the benefit most sought by prospective employees. Hybrid or flexible working was cited by 37 percent of business leaders as a way to attract tech talent, ahead of competitive pay at 35 percent. Some 72 percent said flexible working mattered for attracting younger leaders, and 78 percent believed employers offering hybrid arrangements have an advantage over those that do not.

The piece also touches on AI: four in five CEOs surveyed by IWG said combining AI with hybrid working increased employee productivity, while around 60 percent of US workers and 68 percent of UK workers said AI was improving their hybrid work experience.

Workplace Insight adds an explicit caveat that the figures derive from economic modelling and IWG-commissioned research rather than observed economy-wide productivity gains, so projections depend on assumptions about the links between flexible working, recruitment, retention and productivity. The item is framed as a contribution to the ongoing debate over working location and organisational performance as employers reassess pandemic-era policies.
